title: “EHLO WORLD” - Checking If Your Conversational AI Knows Right from Wrong
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate and validate ethical claims made about conversational AI systems. The authors ask whether ethical behavior in chatbots and similar agents should be governed primarily through top-down regulation, bottom-up technical processes, or a hybrid of the two. The discussion is motivated by concerns about privacy, manipulation, bias, and the social impact of conversational agents in real-world deployments.

Rather than studying an educational intervention or a generative AI tool in a learning setting, the paper is a conceptual framework paper. It uses customer service chatbots as the main example to illustrate how ethical standards might be specified and checked. The paper argues that top-down regulation can define what systems should not do, while bottom-up processes such as bias-checking checklists, certified components, repeatable builds, and automated tests can verify what systems do in practice.

The context is broad commercial conversational AI rather than a specific user population, school level, or country. The main conclusion is that neither regulation nor technical certification alone is sufficient; instead, an interdependent hybrid approach is needed to create small, verifiable claims about chatbot behavior and to better protect users from harmful or manipulative AI outputs.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/position paper about ethics and governance of conversational AI, not an empirical study of educational outcomes. It does not present a research design, sample, or measured effects relevant to middle school mathematics achievement.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on student achievement outcomes and does not evaluate ChatGPT or any generative AI tool in a middle school mathematics context. Its relevance is only indirect, through general discussion of conversational AI ethics and regulation.
